summary.lead: Official summary (Congressional Research Service, Reported to House):

blocks.text: This bill directs the Forest Service, upon the request of the State of Arkansas, to convey the Crossett Experimental Forest, the R.R. Reynolds Research Natural Area, and associated facilities to the state.
Upon the conveyance, Arkansas must designate the land as the Crossett Experimental State Forest. In order to retain the land, Arkansas must
use the land for forest research, education, and demonstration purposes in a manner consistent with the historic research mission of the forest; and

use the forest in coordination with the University of Arkansas at Monticello and the University of Arkansas Division of Agriculture, including by providing the universities with reasonable access to the forest for research and educational purposes.

The bill outlines the terms and conditions of the conveyance, including requiring the conveyance to be (1) subject to valid existing rights, (2) made without consideration (e.g., payment), and (3) made by quitclaim deed.
Arkansas must pay the costs of the conveyance, including costs for surveys and other administrative costs.

The Crossett Experimental Forest Act of 2026 would require the Forest Service, if the State of Arkansas asks, to transfer the Crossett Experimental Forest, the R.R. Reynolds Research Natural Area, and related facilities to the state.

After the transfer, Arkansas would have to name the land the Crossett Experimental State Forest. To keep the land, the state must use it for forest research, education, and demonstration in a way that matches the forest's long-standing research purpose. The state must also work with the University of Arkansas at Monticello and the University of Arkansas Division of Agriculture, including giving the universities reasonable access to the forest for research and teaching.

The transfer would be subject to any valid rights that already exist on the land. Arkansas would receive the land at no cost, and the transfer would be made by quitclaim deed, which passes whatever interest the government holds without a guarantee of clear title. Arkansas would also pay all the costs of the transfer, including surveys and other administrative expenses.
